text:
Pierre, in reply to Natasha’s words, told her how unbearable it had been for him in Petersburg to attend evening parties and dinners with ladies.

“I have quite forgotten how to talk to ladies,” he said. “It is simply boring. Especially since I was so busy.”

Natasha looked intently at him and continued:

“Marie is such a delight!” she said. “How well she understands children. It is as though she sees only their souls. Yesterday, for instance, Mitenka began to be capricious...”

“Oh, how like his father he is,” Pierre interrupted.

Natasha understood why he had made this remark about Mitenka’s resemblance to Nikolai: the memory of his dispute with his brother-in-law was unpleasant to him, and he wanted to know Natasha’s opinion of it.

“Nikolenka has this weakness: if something is not accepted by everyone, he will not agree to it for anything. But I understand that what you particularly value is opening up a new path,” she said, repeating words Pierre had once spoken.

“No, the main thing,” said Pierre, “is that, for Nikolai, ideas and reasoning are an amusement, almost a way of passing the time. There he is building up a library and has made it a rule not to buy a new book before he has read the one he bought—Sismondi, and Rousseau, and Montesquieu,” Pierre added with a smile. “You know how I...” he began, intending to soften his words; but Natasha interrupted him, making it clear that this was unnecessary.

“So you say that, for him, ideas are an amusement...”

“Yes, while for me everything else is an amusement. The whole time I was in Petersburg, I saw everyone as though in a dream. When an idea occupies me, everything else is an amusement.”

“Oh, what a pity I did not see you greeting the children,” said Natasha. “Which of them was happiest to see you? Liza, surely?”

“Yes,” said Pierre, and continued with what occupied his mind. “Nikolai says that we must not think. But I cannot help it. Quite apart from the fact that in Petersburg I felt—I can tell you this—that without me all of it was falling apart, with everyone pulling in his own direction. But I managed to bring them all together, and then my idea is so simple and clear. You see, I am not saying that we ought to oppose this person or that person. We may be mistaken. What I say is: let those who love the good join hands, and let there be one banner—active virtue. Prince Sergei is a splendid man and clever.”

Natasha would not have doubted that Pierre’s idea was a great idea, but one thing troubled her. It was that he was her husband. “Can such an important and necessary man for society also be my husband? How did that happen?” She wanted to express this doubt to him. “Who, exactly, are the people capable of deciding whether he really is so much cleverer than everyone else?” she asked herself, going over in her imagination the people whom Pierre held in very high esteem. Judging by his stories, there was no one in the world whom he respected as much as Platon Karataev.

“Do you know what I am thinking about?” she said. “About Platon Karataev. What about him? Would he approve of you now?”

Pierre was not at all surprised by this question. He understood the course of his wife’s thoughts.

“Platon Karataev?” he said, and became thoughtful, evidently making a sincere effort to imagine Karataev’s judgment on the matter. “He would not have understood, though perhaps he might have approved.”

“I love you terribly!” Natasha said suddenly. “Terribly. Terribly!”

“No, he would not have approved,” said Pierre after thinking. “What he would have approved of is our family life. He so wished to see propriety, happiness, and tranquility in everything, and I would proudly have shown him the two of us. You speak of being apart. But you would not believe what a special feeling I have for you after we have been apart...”

“Oh, there is something else...” Natasha began.

“No, that is not it. I never stop loving you. And it is impossible to love you more; but this is something special... Well, yes...” He did not finish, because their eyes met and said the rest.

“What nonsense,” Natasha said suddenly. “A honeymoon, and the greatest happiness being at the beginning! On the contrary, now is the best time. If only you did not go away. Do you remember how we used to quarrel? And I was always to blame. Always me. And I do not even remember what we quarreled about.”

“Always about the same thing,” said Pierre, smiling. “Jeal—”

“Do not say it; I cannot bear it!” Natasha cried. A cold, angry gleam lit up her eyes. “Did you see her?” she added after a pause.

“No, and even if I had seen her, I would not have recognized her.”

They were silent.

“Oh, do you know? While you were talking in the study, I was looking at you,” Natasha began, evidently trying to drive away the cloud that had come over her. “You are as like him as two drops of water—like the boy. (That was what she called her son.) Oh, it is time for me to go to him... It has come... And I am sorry to leave.”

They were silent for several seconds. Then suddenly, at the same moment, they turned toward each other and began to say something. Pierre began with self-satisfaction and enthusiasm; Natasha, with a quiet, happy smile. Having spoken at once, they both stopped, each yielding to the other.

“No, what is it? Speak, speak.”

“No, you tell me; mine is only nonsense,” said Natasha.

Pierre said what he had begun to say. It was a continuation of his self-satisfied reflections on his success in Petersburg. At that moment it seemed to him that he had been called upon to give a new direction to all Russian society and to the whole world.

“I only wanted to say that all ideas that have enormous consequences are always simple. My whole idea is that if vicious people are united and constitute a force, then honest people need only do the same thing. You see how simple it is.”

“Yes.”

“And what did you want to say?”

“Oh, just nonsense.”

“No, tell me anyway.”

“It was nothing, a trifle,” said Natasha, her smile growing more radiant still. “I only wanted to tell you about Petya: today the nurse came up to take him from me, and he laughed, screwed up his eyes, and pressed himself against me—he must have thought he was hiding. Terribly sweet. There he is, crying. Well, goodbye!” And she left the room.

At the same time, downstairs, in the part of the house occupied by Nikolenka Bolkonsky, a small icon lamp was burning in his bedroom as always (the boy was afraid of the dark, and they had been unable to cure him of this failing). Dessalles was asleep, propped high on his four pillows, and his Roman nose emitted regular sounds of snoring. Nikolenka, who had just awakened, sat on his bed in a cold sweat, his eyes wide open, staring before him. A terrible dream had awakened him. In his dream he had seen himself and Pierre wearing helmets like those depicted in the edition of Plutarch. He and Uncle Pierre were marching at the head of a huge army. This army was composed of white, slanting lines that filled the air like the gossamer threads that fly in autumn and that Dessalles called the Virgin’s thread. Ahead of them was glory, like those same threads, only somewhat denser. They—he and Pierre—were borne lightly and joyfully closer and closer to their goal. Suddenly the threads that moved them began to weaken and become entangled; it became difficult to move. And Uncle Nikolai Ilyich stood before them in a menacing and stern posture.
